newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel vows to make euro as hard as mark.
newsitem.headline: Waigel vows to make euro as hard as mark.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Saturday vowed not to allow Europe's single currency to be weakened by watering down the strict fiscal critieria set out in the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union (EMU).

European Union members will have to rely on fiscal belt-tightening and not political compromises to meet the tough EMU benchmarks in 1997, the crunch year for deciding who will qualify for EMU in 1999.

To ensure the new euro remains as stable as the mark, Europe's anchor currency, Waigel said it was necessary to stick to the EMU criteria and agree on a stability pact with tough sanctions against countries that later break discipline.
"I will make sure that the euro is as hard as the mark," he told the weekly news magazine Der Spiegel in an interview made available ahead of publication on Monday.
"We cannot allow expectations to arise on financial markets that in the end there will be some kind of political compromise that will lead to a softer euro," he added.

At a meeting of European economic and finance ministers last week, Germany appeared to block agreement on a stability pact by insisting on stiff fines for countries that fail to keep the lid on budget deficits after the start of EMU.

Germany's tough stance in Brussels and its insistence on a strict interpretation of the criteria has fuelled speculation that Bonn wants to delay any agreement on a stability pact until 1998 when it is clear who will qualify for EMU.

Queried on this point in the magazine interview, Waigel said, "Indeed, we are not in a hurry. If we don't reach a satisfactory result, then we will continue negotiations after the EU summit in Dublin in December."

Germany's hard-line approach has in part been a response to continued scepticism on the part of its citizens about giving up their strong currency for what many fear could be weaker tender, prone to inflation and curbing spending power.

In a poll published by the Forsa research institute this week, just 15 percent of Germans want Europe's single currency to go ahead on schedule in 1999, with 41 percent opposing the project and 38 percent preferring a postponement.
Garnering domestic support for the European currency has not been helped by Bonn's domestic austerity measures, including tough spending cuts as it puts its own house in order to qualify for EMU.

Waigel dismissed doubts about the government's ability to meet the EMU criteria raised recently by the country's leading economic think-tanks and the government's panel of independent economic advisors.
He said the budget would allow the government to exhaust all borrowing room in 1997 if need be and still get the deficit below the Maastricht limit of three percent of gross domestic product.

Some European politicians have criticised Germany's tough stance as a one-sided interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty that will make it difficult to stem the rising tide of unemployment in the 15-nation bloc.

Former European Commission President Jacques Delors, one of the architects of the 1992 Maastricht Treaty, voiced grave doubts about Germany's drive for a "stability pact", saying it failed to emphasise economic growth and job creation.
"That is not what we agreed to in the Maastricht Treaty," the French socialist said earlier this week.
